channel.description: Personally scored news, world affairs, opinion/analysis & foreign affairs, business & finance, and San Diego/local articles curated by news-filter

item.title: Anthropic Employees Face Tax Challenges with Massive Windfalls
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Anthropic employees could soon be a lot richer. 4 financial advisors share how they can manage the tax bill.
Anthropic employees could face massive wealth from potential IPOs, prompting financial advisors to outline tax strategies. Eric Franklin of Prospero Wealth estimates some employees may see $100 to $200 million gains. Selling shares triggers high taxes, especially in California, where capital gains are taxed up to 37.1%. Advisors warn against immediate diversification, advising employees to calculate financial needs first. Strategies include spreading stock sales over years, tax-loss harvesting, and borrowing against shares to delay taxes. Thomas Kopelman of AllStreet Wealth recommends direct indexing and long-short strategies for larger portfolios. Alex Shahidi of Evoke Advisors highlights psychological approaches, like waiting until stock appreciation covers tax liabilities. Other methods include exchange funds, opportunity zone investments, and buying businesses like car washes or solar companies to generate tax deductions. Advisors caution against DIY approaches, emphasizing the need for professional guidance to navigate complex tax rules and avoid unexpected consequences.

item.title: ATC Routers Cause Nationwide Ground Stop, Investigation Ongoing
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: ATC routers' ability to broadcast data turned off, being investigated: Duffy
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced that air traffic control routers' data broadcasting was disabled after a nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel. The issue stemmed from a router in Arkansas, which officials believe caused instability in the communication system. The router, being examined at a Florida lab, was part of a broader effort to replace copper wiring with fiber cables. Duffy stated that shutting down the routers resolved the problem but emphasized the need to investigate the root cause, including potential user error or faulty hardware. L3Harris, the contractor involved, confirmed its support for the FAA's investigation. Duffy ruled out a cyberattack but acknowledged the possibility of sabotage. He urged Congress to fund a modernization of the aging air traffic control system, citing the need for a new network by 2028. However, Democrats criticized the funding request, noting unspent funds from a previous $12.5 billion allocation.

item.title: Apollo Plans to Slow Hiring Growth Amid AI-Driven Productivity Gains
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Apollo exec says firm plans to lower annual head count growth, mainly because of AI
Apollo Global Management plans to reduce annual headcount growth from 12% to 15% to 3% to 5%, citing AI-driven productivity gains. Scott Kleinman, co-president, stated the shift allows the firm to meet a 20% earnings growth target without hiring as many workers. AI tools enable employees to cover more ground and increase efficiency across operations, according to Kleinman. The company has invested in AI for years but recently saw measurable productivity improvements. Apollo CEO Marc Rowan noted $350 million in planned expenses for technology upgrades. While hiring remains steady in some areas, such as the Austin innovation hub, other firms like Uber and Snap have cited AI as a reason for layoffs. Torsten Sløk, Apollo’s chief economist, acknowledged AI has delivered 'zero financial payoff' outside tech, though Kleinman emphasized AI’s role in reshaping hiring strategies.

item.title: Voyager 1 becomes farthest human-made object after 49 years
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space
NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than any human-made object, reaching a distance of one light-day from Earth. The spacecraft, launched in 1977, will achieve this milestone at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday after 49 years of travel. NASA is celebrating with a public event encouraging people to send the call sign V-G-R in Morse code using flashlights. Voyager 1 overtook Pioneer 10 in 1998 and crossed into interstellar space in 2012. It has conducted flybys of Jupiter and Saturn, discovering Jupiter's faint ring system in 1979 and capturing detailed images of Saturn's rings in 1980. Scientists recently shut down the Low-energy Charged Particles experiment to conserve power, leaving two instruments active. The probe carries the Golden Record, a time capsule with 115 images, natural sounds, and greetings in 35 languages, intended for potential extraterrestrial discovery.

item.title: Sleep deprivation linked to overeating and weight gain
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss
Lack of sleep is linked to overeating and weight gain, according to researchers. A study found that overweight adults who increased sleep by over an hour nightly ate 270 fewer calories daily without dietary changes. Other research shows better sleep correlates with greater weight loss and fat reduction. Poor sleep disrupts hormones, impairs insulin sensitivity, and increases cravings for sweet and salty foods, making weight management harder. Sleep timing and regularity also matter, with consistent sleep schedules being more beneficial than fragmented rest. Researchers note that sleep and diet influence each other: added sugars and refined carbs worsen sleep, while fruits, vegetables, and whole grains improve it. Experts recommend avoiding sugary foods, switching to whole grains, and practicing good sleep hygiene, like maintaining a cool, dark bedroom and regular sleep schedules. Chronic sleep deprivation may require medical attention. The evidence for sleep aiding weight loss is still emerging, but insufficient sleep consistently predicts weight gain.

item.title: Fire forces 18 Oceanside residents, dog to evacuate
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Fire at Oceanside fourplex forces 18 residents, dog to flee
A fire broke out in a four-unit residential building in Oceanside, Calif., on Saturday afternoon. Firefighters arrived at 12:45 p.m. to find the blaze in a first-floor unit of the structure. Battalion Chief Blaine Hensley stated crews deployed hose lines and conducted a search for victims, ensuring all 18 residents and one dog evacuated safely. The fire was contained to the origin area, preventing spread to other units. No injuries were reported. The property manager is helping displaced residents find temporary housing. Carlsbad Fire Department and Oceanside Police Department personnel, including five fire engines, two ladder trucks, and an ambulance, assisted in the response. The cause of the fire remains under investigation. Hensley urged residents to maintain working smoke alarms and have evacuation plans in place.

item.title: Meta's 'Rapture' Date May Lead to Early Retirement for Top Earners
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Meta's 'Rapture' could send wealthy employees into early retirement
Meta's stock surged over 400% since early 2023, turning shares awarded to employees in 2023 into valuable assets. The final payout from these grants is set for February 15, 2027. Andre Nader, a former Meta employee, estimates senior engineers could see annual compensation from stock awards drop more than 40% after this date. Some employees with significant gains from the stock rally—potentially over $2 million—may no longer need to work. The term 'Rapture' has been used by employees to describe the payout date, which could lead to early retirement for those with substantial wealth from the stock surge. The shift highlights how equity grants can become both a financial windfall and a potential exit point for top earners.

item.title: NTSB Links Steering Failure to New Orleans Cruise Ship Collision
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Steering failure preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
A steering failure on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel led to a collision with the American Heritage cruise ship in New Orleans, officials said. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) cited preliminary findings indicating the tanker's steering issue caused the vessel to veer toward the east bank of the Mississippi River. Thirty-two people from the cruise ship were hospitalized with non-critical injuries, though no one was unaccounted for. Investigators noted audio from the tanker's warning system and emergency handling commands minutes before the crash. NTSB investigator Bart Barnum confirmed the rudder remained fixed in a starboard position, but the exact cause of the steering failure remains under review. A preliminary report is expected in 30 days. The collision occurred around 13:30 EST on Friday, prompting rescue efforts by tugboats, police, and officials. The American Heritage, operated by American Cruise Lines, had 129 passengers and crew on board during the eight-day cruise. Authorities shut down river traffic during the rescue as the vessel listed and began taking on water.

item.title: Tanker Attack in Strait of Hormuz Sparks Escalation Amid Stalled U.S.-Iran Talks
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: Iran live updates: Tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO says
A tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Organisation. Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite a June memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the conflict. The war began with U.S.-Israel strikes in February, killing top Iranian officials including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Both sides continue exchanging strikes but at a reduced intensity compared to early stages. The U.S. enforces a naval blockade on Iran's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and accuses the U.S. of attacking shipping there. In Yemen, fighting between Saudi-backed forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensifies, with Houthi attacks targeting Saudi military, oil infrastructure, and transport facilities.

item.title: Ukraine launches largest drone attack on Crimean Bridge
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Ukraine strikes Crimean Bridge in record drone attack
Ukraine launched its largest drone attack since the war began, targeting the Crimean Bridge and other Russian infrastructure. Russia’s defense ministry reported intercepting 2,049 drones in 24 hours, the highest number since the war started. The strike on the Crimean Bridge, a key supply route for Russian forces, followed attacks on 15 Russian regions, including Moscow. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin confirmed 600 drones targeted the city, with most intercepted. Crimea’s pro-Russia governor said traffic over the bridge would be limited, while Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov called the damage minor. Videos showed an explosion and fire on the bridge. Ukrainian forces have attacked the bridge multiple times since 2022, including a 2022 attack that killed five people. President Vladimir Putin condemned the strike as 'terrorism' and vowed retaliation. Zelenskyy warned Russia aimed to divide Ukraine along the Dnipro river, cutting power and disrupting daily life. The bridge, built after Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea, remains a strategic target.

item.title: EU proposes €45bn Ukraine loan tied to budget negotiations
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Brussels to propose €45bn Ukraine loan borrowed against EU budget
The European Commission will propose a €45bn loan to Ukraine, borrowed against the EU’s shared budget, to address Kyiv’s €70bn funding gap for next year. The plan, set for discussion with member states, mirrors last year’s €90bn loan mechanism. However, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria, and others have refused to support future Ukraine financing, prompting German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to threaten withholding EU budget approval unless all countries contribute. The EU summit in Brussels on November 26-27 will debate both Ukraine funding and the 2028-34 budget, linking the issues to prevent future vetoes. Critics, including Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, warn against tying Ukraine support to budget negotiations, arguing it undermines the EU’s autonomy. French far-right leader Marine Le Pen also signaled potential opposition if she wins the 2024 presidential election. Concerns grow as EU elections in Spain, France, Italy, and Poland loom, complicating long-term funding for Ukraine.

item.title: NPR's Student Podcast Challenge Returns for 2027
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: NPR's Student Podcast Challenge is back for 2027
NPR's Student Podcast Challenge returns for its ninth year in 2027, welcoming students in grades four through 12. The competition, which began in 2018, has engaged over 90,000 students, with participants sharing stories on diverse topics. Teachers and students alike praise the program for fostering authentic expression and learning. Laura Frisbie, a middle school teacher, notes the project's impact on students' engagement. Ameya Desai, a two-time winner, emphasizes the value of students sharing personal stories. Submissions open January 4 and are due May 30, with winners announced in September. The contest includes categories for grades five-eight and nine-twelve, plus fourth graders since 2024. Entries must be original student work, with strict rules against adult involvement or copyrighted music. Winners receive certificates, trophies, and potential interviews on NPR programs. Resources and guidelines are provided to help participants create podcasts, with emphasis on originality and adherence to submission rules.

item.title: New World shares drop 40% after $3.2bn rights issue plan
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Hong Kong developer New World’s shares tumble 40% on $3.2bn rights issue plan
New World Development’s shares fell 40% after the company announced a HK$24.9bn ($3.2bn) rights issue at an 80% discount to its previous closing price. The offering, which provides 11 new shares for every existing one at HK$0.90, aims to reduce its HK$150bn debt by HK$40bn-HK$50bn by 2031. CEO Echo Huang emphasized the need to stabilize capital structure amid a record HK$28.1bn loss and property market downturn. The plan allows the Cheng family’s Chow Tai Fook Enterprises to increase its stake to 73% if no external investors subscribe. Independent shareholders will vote in January on the deal and a clause permitting the family to avoid a takeover offer. Offshore lenders will extend debt maturities by two years in exchange for a HK$8.2bn repayment. The move follows a HK$3.35bn payout to exit a troubled airport mall project.

item.title: Sustainable Travel Gains Momentum Amid Overtourism Concerns
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground
Latin America's tourism sector is growing, with South America and Central America seeing 7% and 5% international arrival increases respectively. However, overtourism is causing environmental and social issues, prompting measures like Peru's warning over Machu Picchu's visitor limits and Ecuador's $200 entrance fee for the Galapagos. Experts at ITB Americas highlight shifting trends toward sustainable travel, including smaller group sizes, nature-positive initiatives, and community-based tourism. Richard Bazan of Planeterra notes that even all-inclusive resorts must engage with local environments. Booking.com's 2025 survey found 93% of travelers want sustainable choices, with 53% aware of tourism's social impacts. Sarah Payne of UnTours Foundation stresses financing barriers for local communities, while Sebastian Munoz emphasizes co-designing tours with residents. Bazan advocates market-driven approaches, urging outsiders to amplify local voices rather than impose solutions. Examples like the Mixtec community show cultural revitalization through tourism. Experts agree change is slow but necessary for long-term value and visitor satisfaction.

item.title: Climate ministers divided on final agreement and fossil fuel transition
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Climate ministers start final week of talks deeply divided over age-old issues
Climate ministers at the UN COP31 summit in Antalya are divided on finalizing a global agreement, with disputes over fossil fuel transitions, climate finance, and electrification. Australia, leading negotiations, plans to release a draft agreement this week, but countries remain split on whether to proceed with a cover text. Fossil fuel-dependent nations like India and Saudi Arabia resist commitments to phase out coal, oil, and gas, while others push for stronger action. Turkey proposed a voluntary pledge to increase electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, supported by the UK, Germany, and Finland, though its inclusion in the final text is contested. The EU’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, expressed openness to a pragmatic approach, even if it means accepting 'grey electricity' from polluting sources. Meanwhile, tensions persist over the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), which exporters like India and China argue harms their economies. The summit’s final week focuses on balancing ambitious climate goals with political realities, as negotiators seek consensus amid deep divisions.

item.title: Coalition of the Wiling Aims to Drive Fossil Fuel Phaseout Momentum
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?
COP26 failed to produce a binding fossil fuel phaseout agreement, prompting 57 countries to form a 'coalition of the willing' to accelerate the transition. Their April summit in Santa Marta, Colombia, focused on developing national roadmaps and restructuring financial systems to phase out fossil fuels. Discussions included cutting subsidies and supporting workers in the sector. At COP28 in Turkey, momentum remains uncertain despite a 2023 pledge to transition away from fossil fuels. The coalition aims to build political will and share expertise on implementing transition plans. Germany, France, and the Netherlands have released national fossil fuel phaseout roadmaps, while Brazil's 200-page global roadmap outlines a phased transition by 2033. Critics note ongoing fossil fuel expansion and subsidies totaling $920 billion annually. The coalition's success depends on inclusivity and demonstrating feasibility. Turkey's push for 35% electricity in final energy consumption by 2035 faces scrutiny over clean energy sources. Analysts emphasize the need for renewable-powered electrification to align with phaseout goals.

item.title: San Diego County to Get Two Cool Showers This Week
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: A pair of cool, showery storms will blow through San Diego County this week
San Diego County will experience two cool, showery storms this week. The National Weather Service forecasts the first system to arrive late Monday, lasting into Tuesday, with a second system on Thursday and Friday. Rainfall is expected to total 0.25 to 0.50 inches by weekend, bringing the season’s total to 2.61 inches since October 1—2 inches above normal. Temperatures will drop to 67 degrees by Thursday and Friday, below the seasonal high of 71. The storms may lower the snow level to 6,000 feet, though snowfall will be light and brief. Forecasters note the rain will slowly seep into soil rather than cause flooding.

item.title: Russia allows conscripts to avoid army service by joining drone force
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Russia is letting conscripts dodge army service by joining its drone forces for 1 year
Russia allows men in Moscow to avoid one-year military conscription by joining its Unmanned Systems Forces, a drone warfare branch established in November 2025. Maj. Gen. Maxim Loktev announced the pilot program, stating a one-year contract with the force fulfills compulsory service. Recruitment prioritizes candidates with IT, electronics, or aeromodelling experience. Concerns persist about indefinite contract renewals, as opposition media cites a letter claiming commanders may legally extend service beyond the initial term. The defense ministry insists commanders must follow contract terms, but discharge procedures remain unclear. Reports indicate some recruits were assigned to frontline units, including three students killed in June. Ukraine's own Unmanned Systems Forces, led by Maj. Robert Brovdi, has achieved significant drone strike success. Russia aims to expand its drone branch to 210,000 troops by 2030, with Ukrainian officials estimating its size grew from 10,000 to over 100,000 between 2025 and 2026.

item.title: Jordan bans Telegram over radicalisation linked to church attack
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Jordan bans Telegram app over 'radicalisation' claims
Jordan banned Telegram on Monday, citing concerns over radicalisation linked to a recent church attack. The move follows a deadly shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak on October 23, which killed seven and injured 34. Jordan retaliated with airstrikes on Syria, killing 20 militants and some civilians. A court sentenced three men to death for their involvement in the attack, describing them as hardline Islamist followers. Authorities claim Telegram has been used by Islamic State militants for communication and propaganda. The app's founder, Pavel Durov, denies aiding terrorism, rejecting Russian accusations that Telegram hosts tools for coordinating attacks. Jordan, a stable Middle Eastern ally of the U.S., has also banned TikTok in 2022 over similar claims. Christians make up 3% of Jordan's 10 million population, with the country hosting one of the world's oldest Christian communities.

item.title: Bryan Johnson partners with Tovala to deliver his longevity-focused meals
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Bryan Johnson made a meal delivery service so you can eat like him. Nutritionists have notes.
Bryan Johnson, known for his strict longevity regimen, is partnering with Tovala to offer meal deliveries based on his Blueprint protocol. Meals priced at $14 per plate include options like salmon and kale salad, high-fiber snacks, and 'super veggie' dishes. Johnson faced challenges like lead contamination in lentils and microplastic packaging but claims the result caters to those seeking health without effort. Tovala CEO David Rabie noted the balance between Johnson's strict approach and more moderate dietary preferences. Dietitians praised the meals' nutritional content but warned about high sodium levels, with some recommending supplements like legumes and fermented foods. Both experts agreed meal delivery can aid healthy eating but emphasized consistency and informed choices are key to longevity.

item.title: Taco Bell in Pacifica Stays Open Amid Record Waves
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: 'Vibes remain high' despite massive waves at California's famed oceanside Taco Bell
Monster waves up to 25-30 feet battered California's coast over the weekend, prompting high surf warnings. Despite the conditions, the Pacifica Taco Bell Cantina remained open, with patrons enjoying drinks on its waterfront deck. Social media users expressed concern, with some calling for National Guard assistance and others requesting prayers. A San Francisco Chronicle reporter posted a 'proof of life' video from the location, while an X user noted 'vibes remain high' despite nearby parking lot closures. The restaurant, known for its oceanfront view, serves standard Taco Bell items alongside alcoholic beverages. In 2024, the general manager told The Times that high tides have previously reached under the building, flooding the parking lot. The site regularly experiences high tides, but the establishment continued operations during the recent storm.

item.title: Awesome
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic
SpaceX successfully landed Starship 42 in mid-air for the first time, using the company’s Mechazilla tower arms to catch the rocket after it completed a 22-hour Earth orbit. The maneuver involved deploying over two dozen Starlink satellites, re-entering Earth’s atmosphere at 17,000 mph, and executing a complex flip to vertical orientation. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell called the landing "alien-level technology," while NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman described it as "almost magic." The rocket’s re-entry generated temperatures exceeding 13,000°F, requiring precise engine burns and steering to achieve the correct orientation. Engineers initially doubted the feasibility of mid-air capture, with former SpaceX engineer Tom Mueller recalling skepticism about the "chopstick" landing concept. The achievement marks a milestone in reusable rocket technology, echoing Jules Verne’s 1865 vision of launching spacecraft via cannon-like mechanisms. The success highlights the intersection of audacious engineering and historical literary inspiration, demonstrating humanity’s capacity to turn impossible ideas into reality.

item.title: Pope Leo Tours Amazon, Warns of Environmental and Social Threats
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Pope Leo heads to the Amazon on the final leg of his South American tour
Pope Leo XIV concluded his South American tour with a visit to the Amazon rainforest, warning of environmental destruction threatening both the ecosystem and local communities. In Pucallpa, a deforestation hotspot, he declared the 'cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,' urging Catholics to resist Amazon exploitation. He condemned killings of Indigenous leaders defending their lands, calling the violence 'a cry to God for justice.' The pope highlighted Peru's loss of 3.2 million hectares of forest since 2001 and linked deforestation to water pollution. He also addressed drug trafficking's impact on communities. Indigenous activist Cecilio Soria called the pope's visit an opportunity to voice grievances. Leo acknowledged Afro-Peruvians' historical suffering under slavery, apologizing for the Church's role in transatlantic slavery. He also lamented Peru's political instability, citing a doubled homicide rate and far-right President Keiko Fujimori's election. The pope planned to visit Lima before returning to Rome.

item.title: Sherman Heights Community Seeks to Restore Historic Mural After 50 Years
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Sherman Heights community rallies to restore historic Barrio Sherman Unidos mural after nearly 50 years
A community in Sherman Heights is working to restore the Barrio Sherman Unidos mural, created between 1979 and 1980 by artist Mario Torero. The mural, which symbolizes Chicano self-determination and neighborhood culture, has faded over nearly 50 years. Co-lead organizers Dr. Ismael Carranzo Carrillo and Francisco 'Frankie' Galvan, who grew up near the mural, say it represents the community's roots and future. The last restoration occurred in the early 2000s, but now they seek $10,000 to repair it, with an anonymous donor offering to match donations up to $1,000. The goal is to complete the restoration by 2027. Carranzo Carrillo recalls helping restore it as a child with his parents, emphasizing the need for a community-driven process. The project aims to preserve the mural's legacy as a cultural landmark. Donations can be made via the group's GoFundMe page.
